title: Chapter 14 — One Shoe
text:
<entity repo="place" guid="b17baee9-f904-7bab-a55c-1faa322e89b6">The Roost</entity> was on the fourth floor of a walk-up on Paulina, behind a laundry that had been running since before the city's overlay came online and had never signed up for a feed address. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had come here after jobs that finished clean. After jobs that didn't. After jobs he couldn't yet sort into either pile.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f33a7-ae1e-7e14-b38f-4ab35f598699">Femi</entity> Kasparov was in his chair by the window — right shoe on, left foot bare on the radiator cover, which was warm but not running, the way it always was in late summer. He didn't look up when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> came through the door.

The lemon tree was in the corner. Four feet tall, growing in something that wasn't quite soil, under a lamp that wasn't quite sun. A timer watered it. It got repotted once a year whether it needed it or not. <entity repo="place" guid="b17baee9-f904-7bab-a55c-1faa322e89b6">The Roost</entity> had the wrong climate for a lemon tree. The tree had adapted. It carried two lemons at a time — never more, never less, as if it had decided long ago exactly how much it could hold.

"Chair or wall?" <entity repo="character" guid="019f33a7-ae1e-7e14-b38f-4ab35f598699">Femi</entity> asked.

"Wall," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

He put his back to the wall between the window and the door. <entity repo="character" guid="019f33a7-ae1e-7e14-b38f-4ab35f598699">Femi</entity>'s chair creaked once as he settled. The grow lamp hummed, steady, doing its job.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had come to get one thing tonight, and he wasn't leaving until he had it: a straight answer about whether <entity repo="character" guid="019f33a7-ae1e-7e14-b38f-4ab35f598699">Femi</entity> had known the job on Paulina was rigged before he sent <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> into it. Everything else — the chair, the tree, the bare foot on the radiator — was just the price of asking.

"The medic had come through three days ago. <entity repo="character" guid="019f33a7-ae1e-7e14-b38f-4ab35f598699">Femi</entity> reported it the way he reported everything: once, accurate, in order.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s left hand had been running three degrees colder than his right for the past six weeks. His neuretics had been quietly shifting the load to cope — the kind of adjustment that logged itself and never bothered to warn him. He had noticed it. He just hadn't put a clinical word to it until now.

"She left a number," <entity repo="character" guid="019f33a7-ae1e-7e14-b38f-4ab35f598699">Femi</entity> said. He let it sit a moment. "Two years at current load. Maybe less, if the rate holds where it's been holding."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said nothing.

"She said you knew."

"I knew it was a number," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "I didn't know which one."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f33a7-ae1e-7e14-b38f-4ab35f598699">Femi</entity> considered this. He looked at the lemon tree. One of the two lemons was starting to color, moving from the pale yellow of new growth toward the deeper yellow of something ready. The other was still green.

"Two years is a number," he said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s palm was flat against the wall. He hadn't put it there.

"It's a range," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "She said maybe less."

The coloring lemon turned a little in some draft from the window seam.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took his hand off the wall, deliberately this time, and closed it into a fist to feel where the cold stopped.

"Pull the load off it," he said. "All of it. Reroute to the right side, whatever the neuretics will carry. I'd rather have one good hand than two years of two bad ones."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f33a7-ae1e-7e14-b38f-4ab35f598699">Femi</entity> didn't answer at once. "That's not what she'd tell you to do."

"She left a number, not an order." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the green lemon, the one still deciding. "Start the reroute tonight. I'll spend what I've got where it counts."

Femi's bare foot didn't move on the radiator cover. The metal was still warm from the afternoon, though the system had stopped cycling weeks ago and <entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity> hadn't sent anyone to fix it.

"The medic was thorough," he said. "She ran the full suite. Looked at the degradation curve, looked at the load distribution, looked at what happens if you keep doing jobs the way you've been doing them."

He paused. The grow lamp hummed.

"Then she looked at the extraction cost."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood. The Atlas hardware wasn't just expensive to remove — it was expensive to remove *alive*. A surgeon would have to map every electrode, trace every feedback loop, work through the neuretic integration without triggering cascade failure. Sixteen hours minimum. Specialized equipment. The kind of work that left a trail.

"How much?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"More than you're worth on the open market," Femi said. "Less than you're worth if you stay functional."

It was the kind of answer that sounded like honesty because it was. Femi didn't waste words on anything else.

The lemon tree's timer clicked. A thin line of water started feeding the soil, steady and timed.

"Someone paid for the evaluation," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. It wasn't a question.

"Someone always does." Femi shifted his weight. The chair creaked. "<entity repo="faction" guid="0260c60e-7a18-b1e4-d5f6-a708b9c0d1e2">The Vultures</entity> came by this afternoon. Man in a gray suit, professional manner, didn't touch anything. He had a portfolio with your hardware specs, serial numbers, an Atlas make-and-model line item, and a valuation figure. He was checking it against something in a folder."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s left hand was still a fist. He opened it slowly, feeling the cold gradient from wrist to fingertip.

"The figure was large," Femi continued. "Then he produced a second figure — the same hardware minus the extraction risk. That one was negative."

Negative meant the cost of removal exceeded the salvage value. Negative meant <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hardware was worth more attached to him than separated from him. Negative meant the Vultures couldn't make money on the transaction, which meant they wouldn't come back.

Not yet.

"He wasn't angry about it," Femi said. "He wasn't even disappointed. He looked at the spec, and he looked at me, and he said the numbers didn't work. Like he was sorry. Like it was just arithmetic. Then he left the first figure on the table when he went. The one that made sense. The one that would matter if the extraction got cleaner."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood that too. <entity repo="faction" guid="0260c60e-7a18-b1e4-d5f6-a708b9c0d1e2">The Vultures</entity> weren't contractors. They were a meter. Someone had just taken his measurement and left a number on the table like a promise. *This is what you're worth. When the odds change, we'll be back.*

"Who sent him?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

Femi looked at the lemon tree for a long moment. The green lemon was still green. The yellowing one had darkened another shade, moving toward the color of something ready to fall.

"The message was the Vulture," Femi said. "Not who sent it. The message was: your hardware is collateral now. Your survival is the only thing keeping it valuable. The moment extraction becomes feasible—"

"The moment someone makes it feasible," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> finished.

"Yes."

The water line from the timer thinned and stopped. The soil drank. The timer would cycle again tomorrow at the same hour, whether the tree needed it or not.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pushed off from the wall and walked to the window. Below, Paulina was the city at evening — people moving without urgency, no one looking up, the light starting to flatten toward gold. The laundry was still running. Someone had a radio on in one of the upper floors, music just audible beneath the city's steady hum.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity>," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"She knows about the hardware," Femi said. "She knows about the degradation curve. She knows the Vulture came and what he left."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned back from the window. "And?"

"And she's decided to let you keep it."

The words landed flat. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited for the second part — the condition, the cost, the catch that would make sense of Femi's careful neutrality.

"The debt you carry to her," Femi said, "converts to a different kind of debt now. Not money. Not a timeline. <entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity> doesn't need your cash. She needs to know you'll be useful when she asks."

"I'm already useful," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"You're useful on contract," Femi corrected. "This is different. This is <entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity> deciding your hardware is worth keeping functional because you might be the only person in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> who can do something she hasn't figured out how to do yet."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood. He understood before Femi finished speaking — the neuretics reading ahead, assembling the shape of the trap from the first three corners. <entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity> had just converted his survival into a liability that bound them both. She wasn't protecting him. She was collateralizing him. The Vulture's negative number meant <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stayed alive only as long as <entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity> needed him alive.

The moment that changed—

"She's giving you a choice," Femi said, and his voice had shifted into something that wasn't quite sympathy. "That's the courtesy in sending the Vulture instead of someone else. The choice is whether you take the work she's going to ask for, or whether you make her take back what the Vulture offered."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s left hand had warmed slightly, or maybe he'd just stopped noticing how cold it was.

"What does she want?" he asked.

Femi settled back into his chair. The bare foot stayed on the radiator cover, warm but not running.

"She wants to know if you'll keep working," Femi said. "If you'll keep the hardware running long enough for her to figure out what to do with it."

The lemon tree's leaves caught the angle of the late sun. Two lemons, one ripening, one still green. Both waiting for something to decide their worth.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't answer. He didn't need to. Femi was already reading the answer in the way <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s shoulders had settled, the way his breathing had evened out. The way he'd moved from the wall to the window to standing in the middle of the room like he'd already accepted the terms and was just deciding what they meant.

"Tell her I'll take the work," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"She knows," Femi said. "She already knows."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned toward the door.

"Wait."

Femi's voice stopped him. The old man was still looking at the tree, the radiator, the steady hum of the lamp. Not at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>.

"The medic said something else," Femi said. "At the end. She said the cold in your left hand isn't the hardware failing. It's the hardware adapting. The Atlas spec doesn't carry a learning protocol below the diagnostic layer, and it's found one anyway. It's teaching itself to run on less. She said if you keep pushing, it'll get better at it. She said that's what scares her — the way it was solving a problem it wasn't built to solve."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the doorway. Outside, Paulina was already moving into full dark, the streetlights coming up in sequence like someone turning them on manually, one by one.

"Better at what?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"At running on nothing," Femi said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> left. The door closed behind him. The grow lamp hummed on, steady, doing its job. The lemon tree sat in its corner, carrying exactly two lemons, the way it always did, the way it had learned to, the way it would keep learning until the day someone decided it wasn't worth watering anymore.

The notice had been filed two weeks after the Vulture. <entity repo="character" guid="019f33a7-ae1e-7e14-b38f-4ab35f598699">Femi</entity> took it out of the table drawer — real paper, folded once, the crease gone sharp from sitting.

It came from the <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity>. It wasn't addressed to a person. It was addressed to the building, the way a form is addressed when what it wants is a place, not whoever lives there. The language was flat and standard. The property had been scheduled under the District Acquisition program, WEST TOWN WEST. They called it an *axiom* — the baseline they measured ownership from. It had a reference number. It had an effective date.

The contact name was not <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Mr. Able</entity>.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took the paper. He was still reading it when <entity repo="character" guid="019f33a7-ae1e-7e14-b38f-4ab35f598699">Femi</entity> reached over and took it back — two moves, out of his hand, folded, into the drawer. "Better to read it than log it," <entity repo="character" guid="019f33a7-ae1e-7e14-b38f-4ab35f598699">Femi</entity> said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s overlay had already caught the reference number and the date. He pushed them at the district acquisition database and asked for the rest — the timeline, the assessed value. The answer came back fast: *Access Restricted. District Acquisition Program, WEST TOWN WEST. Dispute window closed. Contact form available. No direct lookup.* He tried another way in. Same wall. The filing was built to be found and not opened — a door with a window in it and no handle on your side.

"Two weeks after the Vulture," <entity repo="character" guid="019f33a7-ae1e-7e14-b38f-4ab35f598699">Femi</entity> said. "They run separate. They don't share notes."

"I know," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

At sixteen, the surgery had taken eleven hours under general anesthetic. Nobody had really asked him. The man he would become — the one people called <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> — hadn't been in the room when they decided what to put inside him, what it would cost a year, what a Vulture would pay for it someday. His body had been changed before anyone asked him a thing.

The <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> was booking the <entity repo="place" guid="b17baee9-f904-7bab-a55c-1faa322e89b6">Roost</entity> the same way. Weighing the asset. Filing the baseline.

He looked at the lemon tree. The one lemon that had been turning was full yellow now.

"How long since anyone asked you about the shoe?" he asked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f33a7-ae1e-7e14-b38f-4ab35f598699">Femi</entity> thought about it. "A while," he said.

Overhead, the grow lamp held its low hum.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move from the wall.

Femi didn't offer anything else. The grow lamp's light lay flat and even over the table.

Femi stood up. He moved slow, his one right shoe making a deliberate sound on the floor. He crossed to the lemon tree and pressed his thumb against the yellow lemon — not hard, just a touch, the way you check a thing you've watched for a long time. He didn't pick it. He went back to his chair and sat with the same care he'd stood up with.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pushed off the wall. He wanted, just once before Femi left for good, to hear the man say something true about himself — to close the eleven-year distance between them with a single answer.

He asked the question before he knew why he was asking it.

"Do you have somewhere to go after?"

Femi looked at him. Not at the question — at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. In eleven years of coming to the <entity repo="place" guid="b17baee9-f904-7bab-a55c-1faa322e89b6">Roost</entity>, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had never asked Femi anything that wasn't work. The question came out anyway.

"There's always somewhere?" Femi asked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> crossed to the tree. He took the lemon off the branch — one hand, careful, the way you take something almost ready. The stem let go without resistance, ready the way it had been for days. It sat in his palm, tight and warm from the lamp.

"You can have it," Femi said. "It was coming off anyway."

He didn't have the gear on him. It was across the hall in his apartment, racked and quiet. He went down the list in his head anyway, the way he had since he was nineteen and first understood what the weight of it meant.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>: a kilo and a half, plain matte-black steel and carbon composite, no edge-work, nothing that needed explaining. It waited in its saya, wrapped and quiet. <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>: the revolver shotgun, heavier than it looked, because everything that worked was heavier than it looked. The mesh under his skin — not gear, really, more like the ground he stood on. Seventy feet of braided polyceramic laid into the tissue of his back and chest, rated to eat 7.62 and mostly succeeding. It had stopped two rounds from the Hegewisch crossroads team three nights ago and still hadn't stopped hurting. The neuretics: Atlas-grade NeoCortex, no governor.

"The mesh stopped them," Femi said from across the room. Not a question.

"Two," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Three would've gone through."

He'd carried the hardware since he was sixteen. He hadn't picked it. He'd woken up with it inside him and spent eleven years turning into the man it needed him to be. The Vulture who'd come to see Femi that afternoon had priced it right. The number he'd come back with was higher than <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> expected.

The number wasn't the strange part. The surprise was.

Eleven years of contracts. Eleven years of pricing himself at the low end of what the market would bear, taking his fee, settling his tab, owing no one — a debt was a handle someone else could grab, and he didn't hand people handles. He'd assumed the work came because he was useful, because he was the only man in the Zone who could do certain things, because the city kept him alive because the city needed him doing them. And all that time he'd been walking around worth far more than he'd ever put on himself, and somewhere in the eleven years he'd stopped noticing.

"How much?" he asked.

Femi didn't answer immediately. He was looking at the lemon tree in the corner, at the yellow fruit hanging full on its branch, the green one below it waiting to be next.

"For the mesh," Femi said. "Just the mesh. Not the Array. The number made me sit down."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt it land. Not shock — he'd stopped being capable of shock somewhere around year three. Recognition. The kind that comes when you realize you've been doing the math wrong for a decade and the error has been compounding.

He needed that number out of Femi — the real figure, and the name behind it. The Vulture doesn't say. That was the whole design: you came in, you priced the asset, you didn't name the buyer, and the buyer stayed clean that way. But someone had looked at the exact configuration buried in his chest and quoted a number too specific to be generic. That wasn't we heard a guy with augments might be selling. That was someone who knew what was in him. Whoever had put a price that high on it had a reason, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> intended to walk out of this room knowing it.

"Femi," he said. "Tell me who's asking. All of it. Now."

He thought about <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>.

Not what to say. Whether to say anything at all.

The night across the hall had been three nights ago. He'd come home from the <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity> job with the tremor running harder than usual — it had been building for six weeks, and that night it went to both hands — and she'd patched the mesh tear and the deep bruising. She'd worked left-handed, economical, no motion wasted, the way she read a system before she read a face. She'd recalibrated that mesh before, tuned the NeoCortex when the threads began to drift. She knew what was inside him better than he did. She knew what it cost. Somewhere after that, the thing between them got said out loud. Named, finally. He wasn't sure which of them let it show first. He'd turned it over twice in three days and landed the same place both times: it didn't matter. It got said because it did. He'd let it.

She knew about the neuretics in general. No governor, Atlas grade, something that would have to be dealt with eventually. They'd never put a date on it, because there hadn't been one. The not-yet had been a vague thing.

Now the not-yet had a date on it.

Two years at this load. Maybe less.

The cold in his left hand wasn't failure. It was adaptation — the system learning to run on less current, better at it every cycle. It sounded like poetry if you didn't understand what it meant and sounded like death if you did. Better at running on nothing.

He didn't know what to do with *maybe*. It was honest, and he respected honest. It was also the word that would land worst if he said it aloud. Not the two years. The uncertainty. The fact that it could be two years or six months, and neither of them would know which until it happened. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> understood numbers. She understood that a degradation curve was a fact, not a problem you solved with optimism. What she'd hate was the part that didn't resolve — the number that wouldn't hold its shape in her hands.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't decided whether to say anything. Standing against Femi's wall in the flat warmth of the lamp, he noticed he still hadn't.

"The <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> letter," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "When's the effective date?"

Femi told him. A month out. End of the fiscal quarter — the way district acquisition always ran. The baseline had already been filed; <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had seen the date on the paper. Thirty days, and then the counter, the grill, the wall where the birds turned on the spit — all of it measured, inventoried, folded into the asset.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> nodded once. "You've got time to repot," he said.

Femi looked at the tree. It was a Meyer lemon. It wanted coastal California, a certain soil, about twice the humidity the <entity repo="place" guid="b17baee9-f904-7bab-a55c-1faa322e89b6">Roost</entity> could hold in <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1706-719b-a8b8-26e0cdd6fb5e">August</entity>.

"<entity repo="place" guid="b17baee9-f904-7bab-a55c-1faa322e89b6">The Roost</entity> was always the wrong climate," Femi said. "The tree doesn't know that."

Behind him, the grow lamp held the tree in its flat light. The leaves had been the same color for three weeks now — <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had watched them long enough to know that stillness was the problem. The lemon was turning yellow on the branch, finishing, but the tree behind it had stopped.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> left.

Femi crossed to the tree and pressed two fingers into the soil, testing whether there was time — whether a month was enough to harden it off for the move. The topsoil crumbled dry. But an inch down the earth held the shape of his fingers, dark and packed, the way it gets when water sits instead of drains. Below that, the roots: circling the pot in a tight, strangled knot, girdling the trunk from the inside. He tipped the pot to be sure. A whole season of leaves he'd read as thriving had been the tree spending itself, hollowing out under the wrong lamp. The soft brown collapse at the base told him the rot had started weeks ago — the second week, if he was honest, back when he'd still thought he had time. There would be no repotting. Whatever he moved to the new district, it wouldn't be this.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went down the three flights with the lemon in his fist, still warm from Femi's lamp.

The ground-floor laundry was still running its last load — warm through the door, the smell of hot clean fabric, a sound in the walls like weather moving in. He pushed out into Paulina. Freight ground along the overhead tier. A Windhover maintenance drone ran its grid circuit forty feet up, orange nav-light blinking every three seconds, and two people under the transit shelter bent over an overlay, laughing at something only they could see.

He stopped on the sidewalk. The atmospheric processors had kicked in around sunset, and the pavement was wet enough to mirror the neon — rain shredded off the lake and dumped east over the industrial blocks, the way it always went. The puddles here were only what the Loop had shed. The lemon was still warm, and his thumb had already found the soft give in the rind. He'd get it to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> one of these nights — put the thing in her hands, so it would stop being only his. Not tonight. Tonight it could ride in his pocket.

Freight moved. The drone finished its arc and turned east. One of the pair threw a shape up into the rain-light with their hands — there and gone — and they laughed again. The city went on around him — the hum of the Substrate overhead, a delivery pod stuttering past at shoulder height, a vendor two blocks down pulling her security mesh shut with both hands, the rattle of it loud enough to cut the ambient — and none of it was about the number.

He put his hands in his coat pockets, the lemon in one of them, small enough to close a fist around and crush without effort. He didn't. He walked south toward <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s was almost empty.

End of service, the hood lamp already down to low, the counter clean except for one other customer hunched over a bowl at the far end. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> hammered the storefront, and the neon from the water recycler next door bled through the glass in a steady pulse — green, green, green. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat. He'd come to eat one last bowl the way he'd eaten a hundred before — to prove to himself the number hadn't changed anything, that he could still sit at this counter and be nobody, still walk out the same man who'd walked in. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> set a bowl in front of him without looking up from the prep surface at her noodle cart at street level, where she was breaking down the last of the aromatics. Pork bone broth, the color of old paper, two hours of reduction in it. He picked up the chopsticks.

He ate the whole bowl.

He wasn't thinking about the number. Or he was, the way you think about a ceiling you've lived under for years — always there, nothing new about it, except now he knew the exact height. The broth was salt and bone and time. It was hot and he ate it slow.

The customer at the far end lifted his head. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt it before he saw it — the particular weight of a man reading a face, matching it against something carried in the pocket, in the memory. The man's spoon had stopped moving. His eyes went to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, then away, then back, doing arithmetic. A phone came out below the counter's edge, held low, angled up. The small betraying tilt of a screen catching a face. Whatever anonymity <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had walked in to reclaim was already gone; the number had followed him here, sat down three stools away, and started taking pictures. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> kept his eyes on the bowl. He could feel the shop's quiet curdling into something that would not let him leave the way he'd come.

She refilled it without being asked. She did that for no one else. He didn't thank her in any way that needed an answer. The shop made its closing sounds around him — the tick of the lamp cooling, the hum of the cold case where the morning's noodles rested, the small rituals that kept the place from falling into entropy.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> turned to the bowl she was rinsing, eyes down.

"Not coming back?" she asked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> set the chopsticks down. "I'll be back."

She went back to the rinsing. He counted the exact fee onto the counter — Φ18, no rounding, nothing extra in it, no mercy in the arithmetic. She didn't look at the amount. She never did. She'd seen a lot of things across the years, and this was just one more. Stood. Walked out into the rain that had started while he ate.

Home.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s light was on, her shadow crossing behind the frosted panel in the rhythm she kept when a job had her — bench to terminal and back, two steps and back, two steps and back. The bench coolers were cycling. Something live under the hood. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the hall a moment and let the ordinary sound of her working land on him. It landed harder than it should have, because he had a number now and she didn't.

He knocked once.

She didn't stop. The rhythm caught for half a beat — coolers kicking on, the two-step picking back up — but she didn't stop. He turned the handle and came in without ceremony, the way you enter a place where you belong. Coat on the peg by her door. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> on the rack above it. He found the corner chair and sat.

She worked. He didn't interrupt. On the bench a coupling seal sat clamped in a vice, thirty-year format, the substrate discontinued so long ago that fixing it meant working with what was already in the room. Her left hand held the probe steady while her right fed current through it, reading the machine's confession in decimal on the secondary screen — impedance values, resistance curves. Her chin tilted, tracking something. Her right hand adjusted the current by a fraction. The readout stopped scrolling.

"There," she said. Not to him. To the machine.

The pipes knocked once in the east wall and went quiet. Two floors up the bird ran its interval — three notes and a rest, three notes and a rest. He listened to it without meaning to.

"You're sitting on something," she said, not turning from the terminal. Her hands kept moving — probe onto the magnetic strip, solder iron up, the tip blooming orange while it waited to be ready. "You come in quiet, you sit in the dark corner, you don't ask what I'm building. That's not visiting. That's waiting."

She touched the iron to a joint and the solder ran like it had been waiting for permission. <entity repo="material" guid="8babfff1-8c0e-4573-e196-efcc8cc5e34e">Silver</entity> line, clean. Then the two-step stopped. She turned in her chair and looked at him, and the look had weight in it — the look of someone owed. "I can make a machine tell me what's wrong. I can open it up and read the circuit. I can't do that with you. So say it, or tell me why you won't? Don't make me pretend I can't feel it filling up the room."

He could have said it from the chair. He didn't. He sat in the warm bench-light and let the building close around the two of them, and kept the number where it was.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went to the terminal.

Not to open the relay. He pulled up the contract log and ran the full eleven years — every job, scope, fee, any tip paid, how long it took, when it closed. He read them in order, timestamp by timestamp, looking for a pattern he suspected was there and couldn't name.

The pattern took four hours to see.

The jobs had come when he was free.

Not when a client needed something. When he could take it. Every one, lined up against his own log, against the gaps between closures: the posting showed up in the relay right when his gear was clean and his body had healed enough to work again. The first job, seventeen days after the last one closed. The next, nineteen. The one after that, sixteen. He scrolled with his fingers moving faster than they should have, because the pattern was already there and he didn't need it spelled out in every entry to know what it meant. The healing window — the span where his neuretics could cycle through a full calibration without pushing the hardware past safe margins. The jobs came in on a timer that matched his body's recovery cycle the way a lock matches a key. He'd been freelance eleven years and had never once gone more than eighteen days without a posting, and the postings always came inside that window. The ones he'd skipped, the times he'd been too torn up to take work, had come through at other hours, and rolled back into the pool for someone hungrier. The timing wasn't random.

He sat with that.

He closed the contract log and opened a blank message in the relay. He looked at the empty field. He didn't type anything. After two minutes he closed it.

He looked at the kitchen drawer. Inside was the printout <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had made three weeks ago — the relay architecture, the scatter of tracked transmission points, all of them closing on the carousel node. He'd looked at it four times. He didn't open the drawer.

He went to bed. The rain was still going past the window. He lay in the dark a long time without sleeping, with the specific sensation of a man who has realized the ground under his feet was never solid — that every step for a decade had been on a surface someone else had been maintaining, and he'd never once looked down to check. The building went quiet by degrees, and the bird upstairs finally stopped, and the rain eased, and he lay there with the number and the pattern and said nothing to either of them.

title: Across the Hall, 02:14
text:
At 02:14 the relay pinged — standard routing, the same client type he'd taken twenty-eight times in the last three years. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the summary. SCOPE and FEE and WINDOW stacked in all-caps, the relay's compression readable in the cadence alone. He knew the fee range before he opened it. He knew the window it was offering him, timed exactly into the space his last closure had left free.

He declined it. Not because the terms were wrong. Not because the job was dirty. He declined it because he'd just read eleven years of contracts and seen that he had never once turned a relay job down, and now that he'd seen it, he could act on it. He didn't type a response. He didn't open the reply field. He closed the window entirely and sat in the dark with the unacknowledged posting still sitting in his queue like a held breath.

That was new.

Across the hall, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s bench coolers cycled down at 02:14.

She'd been at the terminal since eleven. Not the bench work — the prosthetic arm was done and invoiced. She'd moved to the terminal when the building went quiet: the scatter plot on the right monitor, the relay architecture on the left. The same materials she'd worked for three weeks, the cluster tightening every time she cleaned up the transmission signatures. Forty-eight nodes. Thirty-seven of them closing on the carousel at <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> — the node cold now, the cluster still dense. She wasn't a psionic. She didn't need to feel it. She could read the pattern.

She opened the city permit portal. The carousel node was listed under Parks & Rec, maintenance status active; the architecture beneath it registered across a dozen corporate umbrellas, none overlapping, none visible from above. To get down to where the transmission points actually lived you needed paper — a survey authorization official enough that nobody would stop you once you had it. The city's permitting AI didn't flag applications that looked like they knew the system. It flagged the ones that looked lost.

Clybourn Avenue. The center of the cluster, within six feet.

Reason field: electrical conduit inspection, legacy grid node assessment.

She saved the draft without sending it. She'd need a crew — licensed contractors, insurance papers, names on file. She'd get them. She was good at this kind of thing.

She sat with the scatter plot another minute. Forty-eight points of contact around a covered window.

She wasn't waiting for him to ask anymore.

She didn't say anything. The door was a fire door, painted institutional gray, the kind that looks locked because it's supposed to look locked. She pushed it open with one hand flat against the metal bar and held it there, waiting — not an invitation. A statement of fact: *this is where we go now*.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move.

"You already know what I am," she said. Still that level voice, the one he'd been pulling contracts from through a terminal. "You've known since the carousel. You're just deciding whether you care."

His neuretics ran hotter. *Not a problem yet.* But the coal was getting brighter.

"The woman in the alley. Three days ago. You left a photograph." Not a question. He was running the timeline backward: the apartment breach, the tan coat at the carousel park, the six-foot distance she'd held at <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s counter like it was the only safe perimeter she had left. "You wanted me to know you could reach me."

"Yes."

"And now you want me to follow you into a dead relay station because—"

"Because the transmission already went out." She let the door swing shut. It clicked. "Forty-three seconds ago. Your location. Your neuretics fingerprint. Your name."

The rain kept falling. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s breath came out even.

"Who to?"

"The people who've been routing your contracts for eleven years." She stepped inside, into the dark beyond the threshold. "By now that image is in four separate asset files. By the time you finish standing here it'll be in twelve. The people who know exactly what you are and have been waiting for you to figure it out. The people I work for, and the people I just stopped working for about ninety seconds ago."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s left hand was already moving — not for <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>, not yet. For the neuretics kill-switch he'd installed six months back, the one that would fry the array and take the fingerprint with it. It would also burn out the Governor and leave him bleeding from the inside out in approximately six minutes.

"Don't," she said, and the word had weight. "Not yet. You need what I'm about to give you more than you need to disappear. And you need to move."

"Why should I believe—"

"Because I'm the only person in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> who knows what happens when you don't." She was a silhouette now, framed in the doorway's dark. "You don't have until morning. You have until someone with a faster read than you decides to move on the address. And because <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> just locked her counter and walked north, and she's carrying a go-bag that's been under that stall for six years. Which means she's already running."

His neuretics caught it a half-second after his conscious mind registered what she'd said: the relay terminal inside the station, firing up. A low hum, bass-frequency, building. Not old. Not dead. Never dead.

"They're coming," the woman said. "The ones who sent <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> to the dock. The ones who know about <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>. The ones who have been building this moment since you were sixteen years old and they put you in a chair and started making you into exactly the thing they needed you to become."

She stepped back from the threshold.

"Get in or get moving. But you don't get to stand in the rain and pretend you have a third option. Run ground and they catch you on foot in a city that knows your face now. That's a shorter timeline and a worse outcome."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand fell away from the kill-switch. His eyes were still on the amber light on the mast — steady, patient — and for the first time in eleven years, he understood that it had never been a status indicator. It had been a countdown. It had been a clock.

He moved through the door.

Behind him, three blocks north, <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s counter was still lit.

The reflex had already fired — the reach-out-before-going-dark, the location ping he ran through the neuretics before stepping into any building he hadn't cleared — when she turned and faced him. He let it sit, unsent.

"Tomorrow," she said. "This address, this time, the room behind this door. Shielded. Bring nothing electronic you can leave behind — your implant comes because it can't come out. What we're going to talk about can't happen in a room that can hear it."

"Whose room is it?" he asked.

"Mine." A beat. "That used to be a comfort."

The rain worked the awning while he took in what she meant — a fixer who could afford a Faraday cage, telling him the cage was the only place she still trusted. He wanted a name. Not the whole conversation she was dangling for tomorrow — one name, tonight, something to run against the network before he agreed to walk into a room designed to keep him from calling out. Give him that and he'd know whether she was bringing him a problem or making him one.

"You've run forty-one contracts through me," she said. "Eleven this quarter. How many of them do you think came from clients I could sit across a table from?"

He didn't answer. It had never been his to ask. That was the whole arrangement: she vetted the clients, and he never had to.

"I used to know," she said. "That's the conversation."

"Why me?" he asked.

"Because you are the one this concerns," she said. "The rest tomorrow. In the room."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics ran the geometry without asking him to—exit vectors, sight lines, the nearest cover, the thermal read that came back normal, no augmentation signature he could catch, no weapons profile. His eyes caught up a beat behind: tan coat, pale hands, the kind of stillness that comes from someone who has decided not to be remarkable. Not <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s counter. Not the relay terminal. Not anywhere he'd chosen.

He could leave. He could ride home and tell himself the noodle stall had just been a noodle stall, and that what she'd said meant nothing. He wasn't going to. The sentence had already lodged in his chest.

"Tomorrow," he said.

The hood dipped—not a nod, just an acknowledgment. She turned her face to the rain, then stepped past him into the dark of the block. She didn't unlock the building behind her. Three steps and she was gone, the tan coat swallowed by the bad rain the way <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the Gray Zone</entity> swallowed most things at this hour.

The bike was where he'd left it, two blocks south, still wearing the plate he'd ridden down on. He took the long way home. The long way was where he did his thinking. At the second-tier crossing the match landed before he could stop it — voice plus face.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity>.

Seven years of contracts through a cracked terminal. The fixer who paid on time, never haggled, never once handed him work that smelled wrong — which in The Glooms made her rarer than an honest scale. Nobody on the boards had ever seen her face. He'd just spent eleven minutes trying not to look at it.

She'd kept her face off the boards for seven years and then spent it tonight, in the rain, outside a noodle stall. You didn't burn a cover that good unless it had stopped keeping you safe — or unless what came next was worth more than staying hidden. Either way, the weight landed on him.

The bike hummed beneath him at a red light that had stopped meaning anything two years ago. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat through it anyway—old habit, the kind that kept you alive when the city stopped caring about the rules. The rain had thinned to mist. Thermal bloomed off the wet asphalt in his array, a landscape of cooling bodies and exhaust ghosts.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity>. The name sat wrong in his mouth.

Seven years of perfect routing. Forty-seven contracts in eleven years, filtered through a terminal he'd never seen, a sender ID that changed like a tic. He'd accepted the work the way he accepted weather—it arrived, he moved through it, money arrived after. The fixer's identity had never mattered. Fixers didn't matter. Only the work mattered, and whether it paid.

Except <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> had just spent her cover in the rain.

The light changed. He didn't move.

The woman in the tan coat knew his apartment. She'd been outside it at 0314 hours—he'd checked the logs after the breach, found the thermal ghost of a body standing in the alley long enough to verify his window. She'd known the carousel would activate. She'd known before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> did that the sub-basement would sing itself awake at exactly the moment his bike passed the junction. She'd known about <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s counter like it was already on some map she'd memorized.

Which meant <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> had known all of it.

Or <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> had *sent* all of it.

The distinction collapsed into the same answer either way.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulled into traffic. The bike responded like it always did—responsive, eager, the kind of machine that wanted to run. He took the long route home like he'd told himself he would, the thinking route, but thinking wasn't what happened. What happened was the ledger assembling itself without permission.

Contract seven: carousel park. A job that paid wrong, scope that was vague, client attribution that didn't resolve. He'd turned it down.

Three days later, Contract eight: cold-chain pharmaceutical run. Clean money. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> had routed it herself.

The carousel had stayed dormant for years after that. Until the amendment job. Until today.

Contract nineteen: the Cinderfall Anomaly. He'd taken that one. He'd walked into seventeen seconds of 5D bleed and come out the other side with his neuretics still firing. Something had latched then—he'd felt it, a second presence in the stack, something cooperative and wrong.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> had sent that contract too.

Contract thirty-one: the Narrows ramen-ya, the meeting with <entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity>. Not a job contract—a routing message disguised as one. *STANDING ARRANGEMENT: ASSESS COMPLIANCE WITH ONGOING TERMS.* He'd read it as <entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity> testing him. But <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> had scheduled it. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> had put him in that room.

Contract forty-seven: the one with the amendment that broke the formatting. *NO. PROCEED ANYWAY.* And then the lowercase line, the only human thing she'd ever written to him. *received. filed under: firsts.*

Forty-seven contracts. He'd never questioned the gaps between them. Never asked why some months came with three jobs and others came with nothing. Never wondered why the work always positioned him exactly where the next problem would be, like she was reading ahead on a map he couldn't see.

The rain started again. Harder this time. He cut the bike's speed and held the lane.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s counter was still lit when he passed it—that was wrong. She closed at midnight. Always midnight. The rhythm was part of what made it safe, what made it a place where the city couldn't reach him. But tonight the lights were on and the counter was empty, the stool where he sat every night pushed back against the wall at an angle that meant she'd moved it herself. Not in a hurry. Deliberately.

And the go-bag on the shelf behind the register—gray canvas, packed, zipped—that meant she'd known this was coming.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> had told her. Or someone had. Someone in a network <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't known existed until ninety seconds ago.

He rode past without stopping.

<entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity> was three blocks further, his apartment, the second floor where the air still smelled like <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s last project—solder and mineral oil and something electrical that hadn't quite burned out. He could go there. He could sit with the terminal and run the contracts against the timestamps, pull the geometry they'd mapped, see the pattern that had been visible the whole time if he'd known how to look.

Or he could go to the relay station.

The relay station was a dead drop in the sub-basement of an old Axiom facility on the eastern edge of the <entity repo="place" guid="81528864-78de-12ec-5f42-a3179c61adbd">Circuit</entity>. Neutral ground—not his territory, not <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity>'s, not anyone's. The kind of place that existed because both sides needed somewhere to meet that wasn't a threat. He'd used it twice in eleven years, both times for things that couldn't happen in daylight.

She'd said tomorrow. This address, this time.

But <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> had also just told him the transmission was already sent. His location. His fingerprint.
